top_strength: Lukas caught a bad quote nobody was forcing him to catch and fixed it on the spot. Michelle mentioned offhand that "I've got rid of a lot of stuff" and he immediately re-scoped the job — "kind of the quote that was sent over to you is kind of based off of a full home so definitely could make some adjustments from there" — then walked the price from roughly $1,400 down to about $576 and backed it with a real time range for a one-bedroom equivalent. He stacked the right booking removers on top of it ("we don't require any deposit to get you on the schedule" plus free rescheduling if her closing moves) and closed the appointment inside 6.3 minutes. Michelle's "I really appreciate you" was earned.
coaching_note: The re-scope was right, but Lukas priced a 2.5-3 hour job without asking a single question that determines whether it actually lands there. He never asked about boxes, whether she's packed, walk distance, parking, or access at the "back apartment" she's moving into at her parents' place — and on a job quoted this close to the 2.5-hour minimum, any one of those blows the estimate. Ask the probe questions before you drop the number, not after, and explain the clock (on-site start, 2.5-hour minimum, 15-minute increments) so a three-hour quote that runs long doesn't read as a bait-and-switch. One operational flag worth fixing in the confirmation email: he said "the 20th of September, which is this upcoming Sunday" and then "the Sunday the twenty first" in the same call — the booked date needs to be unambiguous.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently polite and patient — he waited out her interruption twice without a hint of impatience — but the warmth stayed transactional: he used her name once, and when she opened up about downsizing, her daughters moving out, and trying to buy a house, he answered "For sure" and moved straight to booking.
